Topic 03

URL Security

A web address can provide clues about a destination, but a URL alone cannot guarantee that a website is safe.

HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP is a protocol used for communication between browsers and web servers. HTTPS uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect the connection. HTTPS can help protect information while it travels between the browser and server, but it does not automatically prove that a site is trustworthy.

HTTP

Does not provide the TLS protection used by HTTPS.

HTTPS

Uses TLS to help protect data in transit and verify the server's certificate.

Common URL Risks

  • Look-alike domains: A domain may use small spelling changes to resemble a legitimate website.
  • Unexpected redirects: A link may send a user to a different destination than expected.
  • URL shorteners: A shortened address may hide the final destination until it is opened or checked.
  • Confusing URL components: Long addresses and extra parameters can make it harder to understand where a link leads.

Safer Browsing Habits

  1. Check the spelling of the domain before entering private information.
  2. Be cautious with unexpected links in messages and emails.
  3. When possible, navigate to a trusted website directly instead of using an unfamiliar link.
  4. Look for HTTPS, but remember that HTTPS does not guarantee that a site is legitimate.
  5. Do not enter passwords or payment information if the destination seems suspicious.
Remember: A familiar-looking URL and an HTTPS connection are useful clues, not proof that a website is safe.
